title: Living in Lahti
subtitle: From your first days to everyday life and Finnish culture.

sections.title: First days
sections.intro: Things to take care of soon after you arrive.

topics.label: Getting to Lahti
topics.summary: Most people arrive in Helsinki by plane or ferry and continue to Lahti by bus or train, about an hour away.

sections.label: By plane
sections.summary: From Helsinki Airport, take the direct bus or a train via Tikkurila.
facts: Direct bus from the airport to Lahti: about 1 h 20 min. Timetables and tickets at Matkahuolto.
Train: go one stop from the airport station to Tikkurila, then change to a train to Lahti (VR).

sections.label: By ferry
sections.summary: Long-distance buses run between the Helsinki ferry terminals and Lahti, or take a train from Helsinki.
facts: Buses from the passenger terminals: check Matkahuolto.
Trains from Helsinki: commuter train Z runs about once an hour and takes about an hour. The fastest long-distance trains take 50 minutes.

sections.label: From elsewhere in Finland
sections.summary: Trains and buses both stop at the Lahti Travel Centre, where you can change between them.
facts: Long-distance trains stop at Lahti railway station.
Regional trains run between Lahti and Riihimäki, Helsinki, Kouvola and Kotka.
Long-distance buses are listed at Matkahuolto.

topics.label: Finding a rental apartment
topics.summary: About 40% of homes in Lahti are rentals. The city-owned Lahden Talot is the easiest to rent from abroad. Private rentals can be cheaper but take more arranging.
facts: Lahden Talot (also student housing): apply on its website, sign the lease online or at its office. Student rooms include electricity, water and Wi-Fi in the rent.
Other landlords include Lumo, Sato, M2-kodit and NAL Asunnot. Vuokraovi and Oikotie list private rentals, which usually ask for a deposit.
Some private landlords want to meet you or show the apartment in person before signing, which is hard to arrange from abroad.
In many rentals you make your own electricity contract and pay for water separately. Check the listing, and set up electricity before you move in.
Free housing and money advice at the Palvelutori service centre (Trio shopping centre, 2nd floor), by appointment.
topics.cost: Lahden Talot: room €350–450, studio about €500, one-bedroom about €600 per month

source.label: City of Lahti: Living in Lahti

topics.label: Residence permit or EU registration
topics.summary: What you need depends on your citizenship. Find yours below. Everyone also registers with DVV afterwards to get a personal identity code.

sections.label: Non-EU citizens
sections.summary: If you study or work in Finland for longer than 90 days, you need a residence permit. Apply before you travel.
facts: Apply online in Enter Finland, then visit a Finnish embassy or consulate to prove your identity and give fingerprints.
Students: the fee is €600 online or €750 on paper (2026). You need €800 a month for living costs (€9,600 in your account for a year or more) and private health insurance.
Applications for studies are handled first. Check current waiting times on Migri's processing times page.
You collect the residence permit card at a collection point in Finland. With a D visa you can travel as soon as the permit is granted.
If the card has no Finnish personal identity code, register with DVV after you arrive.

links.label: Migri: money you need as a student

sections.label: EU, Liechtenstein and Swiss citizens
sections.summary: You don’t need a permit. If you stay longer than 3 months, register your right of residence with Migri once you have moved.
facts: Apply in Enter Finland or on paper, then visit a Migri service point to prove your identity. Bring your passport or ID card and the originals of your attachments.
Students attach proof of studies and show they can support themselves. Workers attach their employment contract.
You can apply only after moving to Finland. Students can apply once their studies have started.
If everything is in order, you may get the certificate at the visit. It stays valid; you never renew it.
Then register with DVV to get a municipality of residence and a permanent address.

links.label: Migri: registering your right of residence

sections.label: Nordic citizens
sections.summary: Citizens of Denmark, Iceland, Norway and Sweden need no permit and no Migri registration. Just register with DVV.

topics.label: Personal identity code (DVV)
topics.summary: You need a Finnish personal identity code for work, banking and most services. If your residence permit didn’t give you one, register with DVV.
steps: Fill in DVV’s online form for registering a foreigner. No login needed.
Book an appointment and visit DVV in person within 1 month of sending the form. Students: first check whether your university has booked a group visit.
Bring the documents listed above. Everyone moving, including children, has to come in person.
Wait for the decision: usually 2–3 weeks if you work or study.
If you meet the conditions, DVV also gives you a municipality of residence. It opens up local services such as healthcare and public transport, often at a lower price.
need: Residence permit card or EU registration certificate

topics.label: Kela and social security
topics.summary: Kela handles basic social security: student, housing, family and unemployment benefits, pensions and health insurance. Whether you qualify depends on your situation, so check with Kela.
facts: Degree students at LAB and LUT pay Kela a student healthcare fee every term. It gives you the student health service FSHS (YTHS) with no charge per visit. Exchange students don’t pay.
Due dates: 15 November for the autumn term and 15 March for the spring term. After that Kela adds a €5 late charge.
Pay in the OmaKela online service. Without Finnish online banking IDs, pay by bank transfer with the details on Kela’s page.
Students covered by social security in another EU or EEA country, Switzerland or the UK don’t pay. Send Kela a photo of your EHIC or GHIC card.
Kela’s Lahti service point is at Kirkkokatu 12.

source.label: Kela: Healthcare fee for students in higher education

topics.label: Money and bank account
topics.summary: Finland uses the euro and most people pay by card or phone. Open a Finnish bank account early: it also gives you online banking IDs, which you use to log in to official services.
facts: The main banks are OP, Nordea, Danske Bank, S-Pankki and Aktia. Each has its own steps for new customers, so check its website first.
Book an appointment as soon as you know your arrival date: the first free time can be weeks or even months away. Branches in Helsinki sometimes have earlier times.
Bring your passport, residence permit card or EU registration certificate, and proof of studies or work. A Finnish personal identity code is not always required for a basic account.
Not every bank gives online banking IDs on every foreign passport. If yours won’t, see Foreigner’s identity card below.
S-Pankki belongs to the S Group: paying with its S-Etukortti Visa card gives you an extra 0.5% back at S Group shops such as S-market and Prisma.

links.label: Financial Supervisory Authority: basic banking services

source.label: City of Lahti: Moving to Lahti

topics.label: Phone number
topics.body: You can buy a prepaid SIM card at kiosks, R-kioski shops, supermarkets and mobile operator stores in the city centre. The main operators are Elisa, DNA and Telia. Bring your passport in case it is requested. Save your address and important phone numbers offline in case mobile data does not work when you arrive.

topics.label: Foreigner’s identity card
topics.summary: The police issue an identity card to foreign citizens who live in Finland permanently. It is a Finnish ID that banks and other services accept.
facts: You must be registered with DVV and have a registered right of residence or a valid residence permit or card.
With it, your bank can give you online banking IDs (strong electronic identification), even if it doesn’t accept your passport.
No card yet? The police can check your identity once and send the result straight to your bank, just for the banking IDs.
Valid for up to five years.
It is not a travel document: you still need your passport to travel.

links.label: Police: identity check for banking IDs

source.label: City of Lahti: Moving to Lahti

topics.label: Getting around
topics.summary: Blue LSL buses cover Lahti and the region. Get on through the front door and touch the card reader with your card, phone or ticket every time you board.
facts: Pay on the bus with a contactless bank card or phone, or buy a mobile ticket in the Waltti Mobiili app. Cash is not accepted.
A ticket is valid for 70 minutes, so you can change buses within that time. Paper tickets from Lahti-Piste don’t include changes.
A season ticket goes on a personal Waltti card and starts the first time you touch the reader with it.
Full-time students pay student prices with a student Waltti card. Bring your ID and student card to LSL customer service.
City bikes (Freebike app) are available until early November, and Lahti has more than 500 km of bicycle paths.

topics.label: Health care and pharmacies
topics.summary: In an emergency, call 112. For urgent advice in the evening, at night or at weekends, call 116 117.
facts: Public healthcare is for people with a permanent address in Finland. Start at your local health centre; it refers you to a specialist if needed.
Private clinics (Mehiläinen, Terveystalo, Pihlajalinna) can be booked without a referral, but you pay. Kela may reimburse a small part.
Medicines are sold only in pharmacies (apteekki), not in supermarkets.
Prescriptions are electronic and work in any Finnish pharmacy with your ID. A prescription from abroad may not be accepted.
Your visit notes, test results and prescriptions are in MyKanta.

source.label: City of Lahti: Health in Lahti

topics.label: Grocery stores
topics.summary: The big chains are K (K-Market, K-Supermarket, K-Citymarket), S (S-market, Prisma, Alepa) and Lidl. Larger shops have the widest selection, and many close earlier on Sundays.
facts: Loyalty programmes K-Plussa and S-Etukortti give discounts and money back.
Most cans and bottles have a deposit: cans €0.15, plastic bottles €0.10–0.40, glass bottles €0.10. Put them in the return machine and use the receipt at the checkout.
Bottles and cans with the deposit mark can go back to any shop’s machine, Lidl included. Lidl’s own plastic bottles go only back to Lidl.
Bottles and cans bought abroad give no deposit.
Estonian, Baltic and Eastern European food: Eestin Elintarvikkeet (Vesijärvenkatu 4) and Baltia Market (Huovilankatu 2).

topics.label: Second-hand shops and bargains
topics.summary: Second-hand shopping is popular in Finland and the cheapest way to furnish a home: furniture, clothes, kitchenware, electronics and much more.
facts: Kierrätyskeskus Patina: Katsastajankatu 14, Kärpänen.
SPR Kontti (Finnish Red Cross): Ajokatu 65, Laune.
Fida Secondhand: Launeenkatu 70, Laune. Furniture, clothes, household goods and hobby supplies.
Online: Tori.fi and local Facebook groups.
Student groups often give away or sell items cheaply at the start and end of a semester.

topics.label: Things to do and free time
topics.summary: Lahti is known for winter sports, lakes and forests. A walk by a lake or through the forest is free and a very Finnish way to spend an afternoon.
facts: Visit Lahti’s event calendar lists concerts, sports, festivals, markets, theatre and exhibitions.
Student events (parties, sitsit, trips) sell tickets in the Kide.app app, and student associations sell memberships there.
Most student events in Lahti are open to both LAB and LUT students.

topics.label: Gyms and sports
topics.summary: Lahti has gym chains, city swimming halls and about 180 km of ski trails. LAB and LUT students get a cheap campus gym through Moveo.
facts: Gym chains in Lahti include Fressi, GoGo Express and Kuntokeskus Liikku. Compare prices and opening hours on their websites.
Students: the Moveo sports pass costs about €30 per semester and includes the campus gym, ball games and group classes.
City swimming halls in Lahti, Kivimaa, Saksala and Nastola, and the outdoor pool Maauimala in summer.
About 180 km of cross-country ski trails and marked hiking trails, many on the Salpausselkä ridges.

links.label: Trails for walking, biking and skiing

topics.label: International House Lahti
topics.summary: International House Lahti helps people who speak languages other than Finnish settle in Lahti.
facts: Guidance in several languages on everyday life, migration and finding the right service.
Regular events for networking and information.
Civic orientation courses in several languages: register through International House Lahti.
Find it at the Palvelutori service centre, 2nd floor of the Trio shopping centre, Aleksanterinkatu 18.

source.label: City of Lahti: International House Lahti

topics.label: Tax card
topics.summary: Get a tax card before you start working. Without one, your employer may withhold up to 60% of your pay.
steps: Request your tax card in the MyTax online service.
If your income or deductions change, request a new tax card with an updated rate.

source.label: City of Lahti: Moving to Lahti

topics.label: Culture
topics.body: Finns value honesty, privacy, nature and equality. People may seem reserved at first, but friendships are often loyal and long-lasting once they develop. Nature is part of everyday life, and spending time outdoors in every season is common.

topics.label: Sauna
topics.body: Sauna is an important part of Finnish life. Many apartment buildings have a shared sauna that residents can book. People usually use the sauna naked in private or same-gender groups, while a towel or swimsuit is fine in mixed company. Sit on a towel or sauna seat cover, drink enough water and listen to your body.

topics.label: Weather throughout the year
topics.body: Summers are bright with very long days, while winters are dark and cold with short days. Spring and autumn can be wet and slippery. Check the weather forecast daily and dress in layers.

topics.label: Getting through your first winter
topics.body: Get warm layers, a good coat, a hat, gloves and shoes with good grip. Wool and similar materials are useful as a layer close to your skin. Wear a reflector in the dark so drivers can see you. Consider getting daylight outdoors and discuss vitamin D with a healthcare professional if you are unsure whether you need a supplement. Be kind to yourself if the dark season affects your mood.

topics.label: Unwritten rules
topics.body: Take your shoes off when entering someone's home. Be on time. Give others some personal space at bus stops and in queues. Buses and trains are usually quiet. Many apartment buildings have quiet hours at night, often from 10 pm to 7 am, so keep noise down. Sort your waste carefully and follow the instructions provided by your building.

topics.label: Useful phrases
topics.body: Hei or Moi: hello. Kiitos: thank you. Ole hyvä: you're welcome / here you go. Anteeksi: excuse me / sorry. Puhutko englantia?: Do you speak English? Kyllä: yes. Ei: no. Moi moi: bye. Kippis: cheers.
